questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Indexing Characters in a String' refers to.
questions.a: Square-bracket indexing reaches any single character of a string: positions count from 0 on the left up to length minus 1, and negative positions count backwards from -1 on the right down to minus the length; an out-of-range position raises IndexError.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Indexing Characters in a String'.
questions.a: The mirror rule is simple: position i from the left equals position i minus size from the right.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Indexing Characters in a String', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: last_index = size - 1

questions.q: How many characters does str1[1:5] of 'Hello World!' return, and what are they? Use the method 'Slice Length Arithmetic'. Work with: first = 60, k = 40, last = 30. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of kept.
questions.a: 0 units

questions.q: How many characters are selected by str1[0:10:3]? Use the method 'Slice Length Arithmetic'. Work with: first = 5, k = 50, last = 80. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of kept.
questions.a: 2 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Slice Length Arithmetic' refers to.
questions.a: The slice str1[n:m] copies characters from position n up to but excluding m, so the copy always holds m minus n characters; a third value k keeps only every k-th one, and the kept count rounds the span up over k.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Slice Length Arithmetic'.
questions.a: A first index larger than the second yields an empty string, and a too-large second index quietly shrinks to the end.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Slice Length Arithmetic', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: kept = (last - first + k - 1) // k

questions.q: Using the method 'Concatenation and Repetition Lengths', work with: copies = 360, first_len = 10, second_len = 100. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of after_rep.
questions.a: 39600 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Concatenation and Repetition Lengths' and work with: copies = 500, first_len = 12, second_len = 200. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of after_rep.
questions.a: 106000 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Concatenation and Repetition Lengths' refers to.
questions.a: Joining two strings with + forms a new string whose length is the sum of both lengths, and repeating with * multiplies the length by the copy count; neither operation changes the original strings.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Concatenation and Repetition Lengths'.
questions.a: Both operators build fresh strings, which is why the originals still print unchanged afterwards.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Concatenation and Repetition Lengths', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: after_rep = (first_len + second_len) * copies

concepts.title: Sum of Digits Hidden in a String

questions.q: Using the method 'Sum of Digits Hidden in a String', work with: code1 = 18, code2 = 75, code3 = 120. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of digit_sum.
questions.a: 69 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Sum of Digits Hidden in a String' and work with: code1 = 100, code2 = 150, code3 = 10. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of digit_sum.
questions.a: 116 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Sum of Digits Hidden in a String' refers to.
questions.a: A string may carry digit characters among letters; each digit character has an ASCII code 48 more than its face value, so subtracting 48 from the code turns the character into its number before the values are totalled.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Sum of Digits Hidden in a String'.
questions.a: Character zero has code 48, so every digit character converts by dropping 48 from its code.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Sum of Digits Hidden in a String', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: digit_sum = (code1 - 48) + (code2 - 48) + (code3 - 48)

concepts.title: Counting Alphabets, Digits and Symbols in a Line

questions.q: Using the method 'Counting Alphabets, Digits and Symbols in a Line', work with: alphabets = 360, digits = 8, spaces = 360, specials = 50. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of total_check.
questions.a: 778 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Counting Alphabets, Digits and Symbols in a Line' and work with: alphabets = 8, digits = 100, spaces = 500, specials = 100. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of total_check.
questions.a: 708 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Counting Alphabets, Digits and Symbols in a Line' refers to.
questions.a: Traversing a line character by character sorts each one into a bucket: alphabets, digits, special symbols or whitespace; adding the four bucket counts must reproduce the total character count returned by len().

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Counting Alphabets, Digits and Symbols in a Line'.
questions.a: A counter that increments inside an if branch per category is the standard pattern for this classification.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Counting Alphabets, Digits and Symbols in a Line', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: total_check = alphabets + digits + specials + spaces

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Built-in Methods for String Manipulation' refers to.
questions.a: Python ships string methods such as upper(), lower(), title(), count(), find(), index(), replace(), split(), join(), partition(), strip() and endswith(); find() answers -1 for a missing substring while index() raises ValueError instead.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Built-in Methods for String Manipulation'.
questions.a: Methods never edit the original string; each one hands back a new value because strings cannot change.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Built-in Methods for String Manipulation', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: str1.count(word) -> occurrences; str1.find(word) -> first index or -1

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Palindrome Check by Two Indices' refers to.
questions.a: A palindrome reads the same in both directions; the check walks one index from the start and one from the end towards the middle, and any mismatched pair proves the string is not a palindrome.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Palindrome Check by Two Indices'.
questions.a: Comparing only half the string suffices, because the two indices meet in the middle.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Palindrome Check by Two Indices', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: front = 0, back = size - 1, move inward until front >= back

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Immutability and Membership of Strings' refers to.
questions.a: A string cannot be edited in place: assigning to one of its positions raises TypeError, so every apparent change builds a new string; the in and not in operators test whether one string occurs inside another, answering True or False.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Immutability and Membership of Strings'.
questions.a: Immutability is the reason methods such as replace() must hand back a fresh string rather than patch the old one.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Immutability and Membership of Strings', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: str1[1] = 'a' -> TypeError; 'Wor' in str1 -> True
